en: Mayon Volcano has steep slopes because its thick, viscous lava cools quickly near the vent instead of flowing far.
Taal Volcano produces violent explosions when rising hot magma contacts the cold water of Taal Lake, rapidly creating expanding steam.
The southwest monsoon brings heavy rain to western Luzon because winds pick up moisture while traveling over the warm West Philippine Sea.
Typhoons gain strength over the Philippine Sea because warm ocean water evaporates, rises, and releases heat energy into the storm system.
Mount Pulag features a sea of clouds because cold high-altitude air condenses the rising moisture from the surrounding lowland forests.
Coastal mangrove forests in Palawan protect shorelines because their dense, tangled root systems absorb and slow down crashing ocean waves.
The Tiwi geothermal plant in Albay generates electricity because underground magma heats groundwater into steam, which then spins large turbines.
The Chocolate Hills in Bohol turn brown during summer because the intense dry heat bakes the grass covering the limestone mounds.
The Cagayan River frequently floods because deforestation upstream causes loose soil to wash down, shallowing the riverbed and reducing water flow.
Farmers irrigate the Banaue Rice Terraces using gravity, which pulls water from protected mountain forests down through bamboo pipes to the paddies.
Corals in the Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park bleach when unusually warm ocean temperatures cause them to expel their symbiotic, food-producing algae.
The amihan brings cool, dry air to the Philippines because winds travel south from the high-pressure Siberian anticyclone over the Asian landmass.
